Adam Clayton Powell Jr. The flamboyant and fearless congressman from Harlem who used his House seat and his pulpit as a minister to challenge racial segregation and poverty.

Powell was elected to the House of Representatives in 1944 from New York's Harlem district and served until 1967, then again from 1969 to 1972. He was also pastor of the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem, one of the nation's most prominent Black congregations, giving him a dual power base in both church and legislature. From 1961 to 1967, he chaired the House Committee on Education and Labor—the first Black chairmanship of a major committee—and pushed through landmark anti-poverty legislation.

Powell was known for his flamboyant lifestyle, bringing his mistress to Europe on congressional junkets and living in a way that provoked the white media's scorn. Yet he was politically vindicated on the charges brought against him. In 1967, he was expelled from the House on ethical grounds, though the Supreme Court later ruled this expulsion unconstitutional. His defiant rhetoric and legislative victories inspired younger civil rights figures, and he coined the phrase "Keep the faith, baby," which became a rallying cry for Black activism.
